problem: The sentence 'a 20-tooth pinion driving a 60-tooth gear makes three times the cycles, because it meets every gear tooth once per revolution' gives the wrong reason. Meshing once per revolution is common to both wheels; the 3× comes from the speed ratio, since the pinion turns three times for each turn of the gear.
fix: 'A 20-tooth pinion driving a 60-tooth gear turns three times for every turn of the gear, so each pinion tooth is loaded three times as often as each gear tooth.'

problem: The figure 200 MPa is the tensile strength of grade FG 200, not its bending (flexural) strength, which is higher. Written as bending strength it can mislead a student comparing it with tooth bending stress.
fix: 'Its tensile strength is low, about 200 MPa for FG 200, and the allowable bending stress used in gear design is lower still.'

problem: A case hardness of 500–600 HV is at the bottom of the nitrided range. Typical gas-nitrided cases reach about 600–750 HV on Cr-Mo steels and above 900 HV on nitriding steels, which is why nitriding is chosen for wear resistance.
fix: 'Case 0.3–0.5 mm at about 600–750 HV (higher on special nitriding steels).'

problem: The 30–50 BHN rule applies to through-hardened pairs. Comparing a case-carburised pinion quoted in HRC with a gear quoted '30–50 BHN softer' mixes two hardness scales and suggests a through-hardness no alloy gear can reach (58 HRC is roughly 650 BHN).
fix: For case-carburised pairs, say the gear is also case-carburised (or through-hardened to a lower hardness) and give both surfaces in HRC, e.g. 'pinion 58–62 HRC with a case-carburised gear at 55–58 HRC', keeping the 30–50 BHN difference for through-hardened pairs only.

problem: 'Reduce the ratio' is offered as a fix for pitting, but a lower ratio only reduces the cycle difference; the lives are still unequal at equal hardness and nothing about the load capacity improves.
fix: Replace with: 'Raise the pinion hardness to about 330–350 BHN, or case-harden both wheels with the pinion slightly harder; do not run equal hardness at a 4:1 ratio.'
